passage: The power went out at eight, and Harish groaned that the whole night was spoiled. The rain outside had already cancelled his picnic that afternoon, and his arms were folded. "Everything is ruined," he said. His mother put out cushions and a plate of biscuits on the living-room floor, but he stayed on the sofa, scowling at the dark window. Lavanya sat up straight in the candle light. "We can't use the tablet, but we can read by this flame, or trade tales, or sing an antakshari round," she said, counting on her fingers, and pulled her grandmother onto the cushions with her. Soon the room was full of singing. Earlier that week, the forecast had warned of a storm, so Vihaan finished his online task early and printed his notes; now he read them calmly by the candle. The day before, when rain washed out the cricket match, the neighbour's children had dragged a carrom board and a ludo set into the hall. "Different game, same fun," one of them said, striking a coin.

qa.q: What time did the power go out?
qa.a: The power went out at eight.

qa.q: How do Harish's reaction and Lavanya's reaction to the power cut differ, and what did each get out of the evening?
qa.a: Harish saw only what was lost and sat apart, so he missed the biscuits and the singing. Lavanya listed what was still possible, and she ended up singing with her grandmother.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling as he sat scowling at the window?
qa.a: Harish was angry and disappointed about his rained-off picnic and the dark evening, so he refused to join in.

qa.q: What could Harish's mother say or do to bring him into the evening?
qa.a: She could invite him to choose the first song or story, without pushing, so his disappointment is heard and he has a role in the fun. He might then see the evening as a different kind of day. 🙂

grounding: Children meet rain and a power cut by sulking, by listing what is still possible, by preparing early, and by switching to indoor games.
